title: The Hidden Cost of Leading Through Fear
author: Joel Salinas
summary: Salinas contends that leaders are tempted to stoke anxiety because pessimism spreads fast and does spark short-term movement, but sustained fear produces mistrust, fatigue, cynicism and burnout. Using Hans Rosling's Factfulness, he argues that a constant drumbeat of negative news leaves people with a distorted, stressful view of the world, and he calls the resulting cycle the Pessimism Loop. His remedy is grounded optimism: name reality and pain honestly, but frame problems inside a larger narrative of possibility and celebrate small wins. He draws on his experience leading through a pandemic and funding cuts at a humanitarian organisation. A closing aside on AI as a leveller for under-resourced nonprofit and church leaders is tangential to the main argument.
points: Fear motivates only until it paralyses, and prolonged alarm turns urgency into drain, cynicism and burnout.
Rosling's Factfulness explains why teams feel more threatened than the facts warrant, since good news gets little airtime.
Optimism is positioned as strategic, not soft: pessimism makes people reactive while optimism makes them creative.
Leaders should tell the whole truth, naming reality and pain while also casting vision and celebrating small wins.
Constantly triggering alarm bells makes teams tune out, so the leader's tone is itself a management tool.
quotes: Fear creates friction, the kind that can ignite a spark in the short term. But if you lead with fear for too long, you don’t just get movement.
Pessimism plays to our brain’s wiring. The human mind is naturally loss-averse; we notice threats more than progress.
You and I know it, urgent works for a time, but only doing the urgent long-term is like running a marathon with a 100-meter dash strategy. It won’t work.
What it creates is chronic anxiety, and quickly puts an expiration date on your team.
Optimism doesn't mean ignoring pain. It means refusing to let despair define the whole story.

The cultural water we’re swimming in is full of fear, and it’s easy to mistake anxiety for action. But when a leader constantly triggers alarm bells, the team stops listening or, worse, starts tuning out entirely.
As leaders, it’s our job to tell the whole truth, not just the hard parts. That means we name reality, but also cast vision.
